title: The chameleon on the tree
hookLine: three friends argue about the color of a lizard on a tree, and the man who lives under it settles it
carry: god with form, and beyond every form
tomorrow: what did a young man from that room tell Chicago?
last: THE SALT DOLL AND THE OCEAN.

cards: Red. I saw it myself, it was red. No, it was green, I was standing right there.

You're both wrong, it was blue. Three friends, one tree, one small lizard, and an argument getting louder by the minute. Each of them went into the woods, saw a chameleon on a branch, and came back certain.
Ramakrishna told this story to the visitors in his room at Dakshineswar, and the one who settles it isn't any of the three.

teach.b: In the Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna, they all walk back to the tree to settle it. A man sitting underneath says: I live here, and I know that creature well.

teach.h: EVERY ONE OF YOU IS RIGHT.
teach.b: Every one of you is right. Sometimes it's red, sometimes green, sometimes yellow or blue. And sometimes it has no color at all.

The one who thinks of God constantly comes to know God's real nature, and knows that God shows himself to seekers in many forms and aspects: with qualities, and then again without any. Hindus have names for both.
Saguna: God with qualities, the Krishna you can dress, feed and sing to. Nirguna: God beyond every quality and every name. Ramakrishna wouldn't let either side throw out the other.
It's the others, he says, who suffer through useless arguments. Notice what the man under the tree does not say. He doesn't tell anyone they made it up.
Each friend really did see red, or green. The trouble came with one extra word: only. And his knowledge comes not from a sharper argument but from living there: closeness, not cleverness.
His last words, sometimes no color at all, point to where the doll went.

It began with Mira's jewel of the name, went out into the lanes of Bengal with Chaitanya's drums, and came to rest at Dakshineswar, where a priest answered questions with a pond, a snake, a doll made of salt, and a lizard on a tree.

how: Ramakrishna's parables, like the chameleon on the tree, are retold in talks at Ramakrishna order centers, in study circles that read the Gospel together, and at home.

o: a mystic of Dakshineswar who taught in parables
a debater well-known for winning arguments on God
a court poet who collected old fables for kings

games.q: the lizard on the tree — tap the pairs.
p: each saw one color and took it for the whole
lives there and knows the creature well
God with qualities, the many colors
God beyond every quality: no color

s: the man under the tree said only one friend was right
he told them every one of their descriptions was true.
he said the creature sometimes has no color at all
for Ramakrishna, God has qualities, and then again has none.
the man under the tree settled it by out-arguing the friends
he knew the creature because he lived there; it's the others who suffer through useless arguments.

games.q: you live under the tree. three friends arrive, arguing whether the lizard is red, green or blue. what do you tell them?
o: it's red. the other two are mistaken.
every one of you is right, and sometimes it has no color at all.
lizards don't change color. you imagined it.
games.why: the man under the tree says all their descriptions are true. Ramakrishna's point: the one who thinks of God constantly knows God shows many forms, and is also beyond them.

practice: Pray today to God in the form you love: a picture or murti of Krishna, Shiva or the Mother, or a name, if that's your way. Then close your eyes and rest a moment in the silence beyond the picture, the part with no color at all.
Then bring to mind someone who sees God differently from you, and ask quietly what they saw from where they were standing. If you don't pray, do the last part only.

wordCard.voice: Ramakrishna. The priest of Dakshineswar, telling of a lizard on a tree that shows every color, and sometimes no color at all.

carryVoice: Your line: God with form, and beyond every form. Tomorrow, one of the young men from that room speaks a long way from home. Day nine hundred thirty-eight, done.
